tweets.text: If you've ever wondered why smart TVs are so cheap, this is why. @log4j rooted his Samsung and found an always-on hot mic, automatic content recognition, geolocation, network mapping, ad targeting and user profiling, shared with Samsung's "400 partners". A lot of it can be blocked in <15 min, wrote a basic guide below. What your TV is doing The main culprit is ACR (automatic content recognition). Your TV screenshots what's on screen, fingerprints it, and sends it home to build your ad profile. Samsung does it every 500ms, LG every 10ms [1]. What is insane: it happens on connected devices too. Plug in your laptop, your console, your work machine, and your TV can fingerprint that via HDMI [1]. He also found that if your Samsung doesn't have a mic, it'll look for one from a connected soundbar or bluetooth device. nitterk.kareem.one/log4j/status/211376224… It's on by default, and you likely agreed to it on the setup screen you clicked through in 10 seconds. Step 1: Turn off ACR Samsung: Terms & Privacy → Viewing Information Services LG: Live Plus Vizio: Viewing Data Roku: "Use info from TV inputs" Sony/Google TV: Samba Interactive TV Menus vary by model, but those are the names to look for. While you're in there, opt out of interest-based ads, reset your advertising ID, decline every optional privacy agreement, turn off voice recognition, and delete apps you never open. Step 2: Give smart devices their own network Put the TV, cameras, speakers and vacuum on your router's guest/IoT network. The logic is simple: these devices rarely get patched. If one gets compromised (getting drastically more frequent with AI), it shouldn't be able to see your other devices or home network. Step 3: Block trackers for the whole house with DNS-level filtering NextDNS (cloud-based) is easy and has a solid free plan. Pi-hole is a little bit more work if you prefer self hosting. For simplicity we'll focus on the former. 1. Sign up at nextdns.io (free tier is plenty) 2. Privacy tab: add a blocklist (OISD is a good bet) and turn on Native Tracking Protection for Samsung, LG, Roku, Amazon (see attached image) 3. Setup tab: copy your endpoint 4. Paste it into your router's DNS settings as DNS-over-HTTPS/TLS (or use the IPs + "Link IP" if your router only does plain DNS) 5. Bonus: block outbound port 53 except to your router. Some devices hardcode their own DNS to get around you Then open the NextDNS logs and watch how often your TV phones home. It's eye-opening. If an app or update breaks, find the domain in the logs and allowlist it. Why they do this TV prices are down 97% since 2000 [2]. Most of that is better manufacturing and brutal competition. But once margins on the hardware hit zero, the cost moved to you. In Q3 2024, Vizio lost $6.7M selling TVs and made $115.8M in gross profit from ads and viewing data [3]. They've said on earnings calls that they keep TV prices low to grow the audience they sell to advertisers. Walmart bought them in 2024. This isn't a conspiracy theory either. Vizio paid $2.2M to the FTC in 2017 for tracking 11 million TVs without consent. Last December, Texas sued Samsung, LG, Sony, Hisense and TCL over ACR. Samsung and LG have since agreed to stop collecting that data without explicit consent [4]. TL;DR 1. ACR off 2. Ads + voice off 3. Smart devices on their own network 4. NextDNS filtering on the router Sources: [1] ACR study: arxiv.org/abs/2409.06203 [2] Cost of US consumer goods: aei.org/economics/chart-of-t… [3] Vizio Q3 2024: sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… [4] Texas v. Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while. The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal. So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time. Andrej Karpathy (@karpathy) Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability. The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. This is a group of reactions laughing at various quirks of the models, hallucinations, etc. Yes I also saw the viral videos of OpenAI's Advanced Voice mode fumbling simple queries like "should I drive or walk to the carwash". The thing is that these free and old/deprecated models don't reflect the capability in the latest round of state of the art agentic models of this year, especially OpenAI Codex and Claude Code. But that brings me to the second issue. Even if people paid $200/month to use the state of the art models, a lot of the capabilities are relatively "peaky" in highly technical areas. Typical queries around search, writing, advice, etc. are *not* the domain that has made the most noticeable and dramatic strides in capability. Partly, this is due to the technical details of reinforcement learning and its use of verifiable rewards. But partly, it's also because these use cases are not sufficiently prioritized by the companies in their hillclimbing because they don't lead to as much $$$ value. The goldmines are elsewhere, and the focus comes along. So that brings me to the second group of people, who *both* 1) pay for and use the state of the art frontier agentic models (OpenAI Codex / Claude Code) and 2) do so professionally in technical domains like programming, math and research. This group of people is subject to the highest amount of "AI Psychosis" because the recent improvements in these domains as of this year have been nothing short of staggering. When you hand a computer terminal to one of these models, you can now watch them melt programming problems that you'd normally expect to take days/weeks of work. It's this second group of people that assigns a much greater gravity to the capabilities, their slope, and various cyber-related repercussions. TLDR the people in these two groups are speaking past each other. It really is simultaneously the case that OpenAI's free and I think slightly orphaned (?) "Advanced Voice Mode" will fumble the dumbest questions in your Instagram's reels and *at the same time*, OpenAI's highest-tier and paid Codex model will go off for 1 hour to coherently restructure an entire code base, or find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. This part really works and has made dramatic strides because 2 properties: 1) these domains offer explicit reward functions that are verifiable meaning they are easily amenable to reinforcement learning training (e.g. unit tests passed yes or no, in contrast to writing, which is much harder to explicitly judge), but also 2) they are a lot more valuable in b2b settings, meaning that the biggest fraction of the team is focused on improving them. So here we are. — https://nitter.kareem.one/karpathy/status/2042334451611693415#m

We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks: Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better: Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better: Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better: Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work! In summary: - As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding. - Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

Anthropic has filed for a record $2 trillion IPO. In a talk uploaded November 30, 2025, a stockbroker asked Elon Musk which company he would buy. Musk said he has no portfolio, then named Google and Nvidia. The man asking is Nikhil Kamath, who told Musk his primary job is stockbroker and stock investor. Musk runs Tesla, SpaceX, xAI and X, and says the output of AI and robotics "will dwarf everything else." The clip is three moments from a 114-minute conversation. The full talk is free on YouTube. In it Musk says US deficits run on the order of $2 trillion a year, and that interest payments on the debt exceed the entire US military budget. His rules for money fit on a napkin. Judge the product, not the price. His test for any stock: do you like what the company makes, do you like the roadmap, do you believe in the team. A company, he says, is a group of people assembled to make products and services. Expect the swings. That test does not solve for daily moves, which he admits are sometimes pretty extreme. His advice is to hold and not worry about them. Watch the ratio. Inflation, he says, is goods and services output against growth in the money supply. AI has not yet raised output enough. He guesses output growth passes money growth in about three years. Know the fix on offer. He says the only thing that can solve the US debt is AI and robotics. That is a bet, and he says so. Money is a tool. He calls it an information system for labor allocation. A trillion dollars on a desert island buys nothing, because there is no labor to allocate. Check who owns it. When he says AI, robotics and maybe spaceflight will hold almost all the value, he runs companies in each of those fields. "I don't look for things to invest in. I just try to build things." Listen from 86:12. Before you buy into any IPO this month, write down what the company sells, what it ships next and who builds it. If you cannot fill in all three lines, you are not investing. You are buying a headline with your name on it. Video

After SpaceX's very first Falcon 1 rocket failed in March 2006, the team was exhausted and heartbroken. Elon Musk instead of only pushing harder, spent more than $100,000 to book a private Zero-G flight, so his engineers could finally float weightless and get a real taste of the spaceflight they were working so hard to make possible. Many of them had joined SpaceX dreaming of becoming astronauts one day, and I love that in one of the hardest moments for the young company, Elon reminded them why they had started in the first place. Elon understood that people building the future also need to feel it, even if only for a few seconds at a time.

I’m starting a new early-stage AI fund, doing what I love: partnering with founders from company formation on bold bets, long before consensus. The fund’s LPs will include Sequoia, Jeff Dean, Sachin Katti, Philip Wong (my Stanford professor and Chief Scientist adviser to TSMC), and others whose work has shaped our industry and how I think about AI’s future. I’ll remain a partner at Sequoia and keep serving on my boards on Sequoia’s behalf. Sequoia has been my home for the past 11 years. I joined as the youngest investor the firm had ever hired. I grew up here. Through years of intense debate and shared work, I found lifelong mentors and friends who took me under their wing and taught me this craft. They taught me to aim high and take big swings. I’ll carry that into what I build: outsized ambition, relentless truth-seeking and curiosity, and a refusal to become complacent. Working alongside founders has made me want to build something of my own: a firm shaped from day one around the convictions I’ve developed over the past decade. Life has taught me not to take time for granted. This is how I want to spend mine. Why now We’re seeing a new way of building companies in today’s AI era. Research and products often advance together. A breakthrough can open a market or accelerate a business far faster than expected. Some companies require extraordinary capital and compute early on. Others reach meaningful scale with remarkably small teams. The rules for how big these businesses can get, and how fast, are being rewritten. But early on, the technology is unproven, the resources required enormous, and the vision seemingly implausible. This is what I love most: seeing the potential right from the beginning, and helping founders realize their full scale of ambition. More than ever, it starts with an extreme willingness to believe early, with bold, independent conviction in a founder’s technical insight before any product or market validation. Then, it means helping founders take the biggest swings, giving the rare, long-term patience to see those bets through uncertainty, ambiguity, and turbulence, and serving as a level head when the stakes are highest. I learned this kind of partnership at Sequoia. It’s the foundation of the firm I’m building. Believing before consensus My fascination with AI’s potential took root at Stanford in the early-to-mid 2010s, studying computer science and working in Andrew Ng’s lab. The friendships I formed connected me to a community whose people and ideas would help shape modern AI and build some of our generation’s defining companies. What stayed with me was the gap between what those people saw was possible and what the wider world could imagine. I’m drawn to founders pursuing ambitions that sound impossible today. I start with a simple question: “What if everything goes right?” Then we work backward together to make it happen. In 2023, Deepak and Abhinav set out to build a general-purpose robot brain at @SkildAI , before physical AI was a consensus bet. Their sim-to-real breakthroughs gave me conviction where earlier robotics approaches had fallen short. But the data flywheel required deployment at scale. We made commercialization as urgent as research and brought in strategic partners like NVIDIA and SoftBank to support the ambition. Three years in, Skild is advancing the frontier of physical AI with nine figures in annualized revenue. In 2024, Ioannis and Misha founded @reflection_ai with an insight into scaling reinforcement learning. As that grew into the ambition to build a Western frontier lab for open models, the hard question was how a startup competes with labs spending tens of billions. An introduction to NVIDIA and many compute calls and recruiting events later, the team has built Beam, now one of the leading US open models. In 2025, Anna and Azalia, the co-creators of AlphaChip, founded @RicursiveAI to design models and hardware together. From day one, we made early customers and ecosystem partners a priority. Today, they are showing order-of-magnitude improvements on real workloads, working with some of the industry’s most consequential players, and reaching a defining inflection point. The ambition keeps growing as these companies scale. @linear has always had a kind of magic to it. Now it’s the system a new generation of AI companies builds on, for teams and agents alike. @tavus saw early that we’d one day talk to AI the way we talk to each other. Today, it’s building the human computing interface for a world of AI colleagues. @Mach_Industries began as hydrogen experiments in an MIT dorm room. It has since become one of the most exciting next-generation defense companies. Making the ambition possible Being a first believer is only the beginning. Compute falls through. A deep-pocketed incumbent makes your mission its top priority. A breakthrough changes the opportunity and the capital required overnight. These are stomach-churning moments, and early belief carries a responsibility to help make the bet work. This is the partnership I love: turning the full ambition into concrete steps. Raising capital, securing compute and strategic partners, recruiting exceptional people, and winning the first customers together. Thinking several moves ahead while solving what’s in front of us. And as breakthroughs open new possibilities, helping founders dream even bigger. Thank you To the founders I’ve worked with: thank you for trusting me and Sequoia to be your first partner and first believer. It’s been the joy of a lifetime, and I can’t wait to keep building together. Thank you to Alfred and Pat for your leadership of Sequoia and your support of my next chapter. To Roelof, for bringing me into Sequoia and believing in me from the beginning. Alfred and Roelof, you have been mentors in investing and in life. So much of what I know, and the investor I’ve become, comes from your guidance and generosity over the years. To Bill, for the close partnership and wealth of knowledge, always wrapped in humility. To Shaun, for showing me how to think deeply and imaginatively. To Michael Moritz, for inspiring 22-year-old me to dream big. To Doug, for teaching me to keep things simple. To Bogie and Jess, for bringing joy to the everyday and perspective on what matters. And to all my Sequoia teammates, for the friendship, camaraderie, and lessons I’ll carry with me. To my family, especially my husband and my brother, who have each started companies of their own: thank you for giving me the courage to take this leap. Let’s get to work!

The newsletter industry lacks innovation Look at mobile apps, ecom, edtech. Custom quiz onboarding, a landing page for every ad, hundreds of new creatives a day. An agent repeats a mistake, so you add a rule. Months later, nobody remembers why it exists. “Why Does CLAUDE.md Keep Growing?” calls this “catastrophic remembering.” The study tracks 247,694 instruction lifetimes across 1,867 repositories. Files like CLAUDE.md more than triple over their lifetime. The cause is lost reasoning, not changing requirements. Without the reason, deleting anything feels risky. The paper tests attaching a comment to each rule. Those comments record: > The failure behind the instruction > The hypothesis behind the fix > Evidence from previous attempts The author built tests where the ideal prompt was known. Uncommented prompts ended 211% longer than that ideal. Informative comments cut the excess to 1.4%. The agent followed constraints equally well both ways. In an interview with AlphaSignal, author Kushal Chakrabarti ( @kushalc ) recommends a cache approach. “The cache should have triggers and pointers, not summaries.”

processed.summary: Cette journée de veille IA met en lumière la dichotomie entre les attentes du grand public et les capacités avancées des IA de pointe, notamment dans des domaines techniques comme le code et les mathématiques. Elle souligne aussi l'importance cruciale de la vie privée face à nos appareils connectés et l'émergence de nouvelles manières d'interagir avec les IA, qui vont au-delà du texte pour inclure des médias riches. Enfin, de nombreuses annonces de modèles et d'outils performants sont faites, tout en soulignant la nécessité de développer des IA plus sûres et éthiques.

glossaire.definition: Un programme informatique très avancé capable de comprendre et de générer du texte, comme un cerveau géant qui a lu énormément de livres et de pages web.

Une intelligence artificielle qui peut agir de manière autonome pour accomplir des tâches complexes, en décomposant les problèmes et en utilisant des outils, allant bien au-delà de la simple conversation.
Une méthode d'IA où un programme apprend à améliorer ses performances en interagissant avec son environnement et en recevant des récompenses ou des pénalités pour ses actions.
Se dit d'un modèle d'IA dont les 'poids' (les paramètres internes appris par le modèle) sont rendus publics, ce qui permet à la communauté de l'utiliser et de l'étudier librement.
Un ensemble de tests standardisés utilisé pour évaluer et comparer les performances de différents systèmes ou modèles d'IA sur des tâches spécifiques.
C'est quand un modèle d'IA génère des informations incorrectes, inventées ou sans rapport avec les faits, mais les présente comme vraies.
La quantité maximale de texte qu'un modèle d'IA peut 'voir' ou traiter en une seule fois pour comprendre une requête et générer une réponse.

highlights.text_fr: Je dépoussière ce tweet d'avril parce que ce fossé de compréhension des capacités des LLM *s'élargit*. Ce n'est plus "deux groupes de personnes qui parlent sans se comprendre" mais plutôt un entonnoir très étroit. - On estime à environ 6 milliards de personnes (environ 75% de la population) qui n'ont presque pas été en contact avec les LLM. - Environ 1 à 2 milliards (~20%) sont des utilisateurs occasionnels et peu fréquents de produits gratuits de type ChatGPT. Ce groupe voit des chatbots un peu maladroits et les traite comme une meilleure recherche Google, une aide à l'écriture, etc. Peut-être qu'un agent essaie de vous réserver un vol. J'ai des amis non-techniciens qui (raisonnablement, à mon avis) disent qu'ils n'y voient pas beaucoup d'utilité. Même de nombreux professionnels en dehors des mathématiques et du code sont à ce niveau. Par exemple, les dirigeants et de nombreuses autres fonctions passent beaucoup de leur temps à parler à d'autres personnes, donc même s'ils comprennent intellectuellement ce qui se passe, c'est de seconde main et un peu abstrait. - Nous arrivons maintenant à l'utilisation professionnelle des LLM de pointe dans les mathématiques et le code. Quelque part autour de 20 millions de personnes (0,2%) voient directement que de grands projets complexes qui leur prenaient des semaines/mois peuvent maintenant être réalisés par des agents avec une simple instruction (un "prompt"). Construire des applications, copier des applications, traduire des applications, décompiler des applications à partir de binaires... Tout cela s'est produit très rapidement et récemment – il y a moins d'un an, j'écrivais du code manuellement, tapant des commandes informatiques mémorisées dans un éditeur de code caractère par caractère, appuyant occasionnellement sur Tab pour compléter un petit morceau de code. - Et enfin, nous arrivons aux quelque 5 000 personnes (~0,00006%) ayant accès à des systèmes de pointe en interne. Le monde extérieur a vu l'aperçu. Cela ressemble à des essaims de milliers d'agents collaborant pendant des semaines sur des mégaprojets logiciels : création de failles "zero days", exécution de cyberattaques et de défenses à la vitesse de la machine, découverte de nouvelles sciences, avancement de la frontière des mathématiques. Des choses qui auraient pris des années de travail aux meilleurs professionnels de l'industrie. Pendant ce temps, l'examen et la compréhension humaine commencent à prendre du retard. Par exemple, les gens sont toujours impliqués dans "l'archéologie" de l'incident OpenAI-HF d'il y a plusieurs mois. Les mathématiciens pourraient se pencher sur les 722 manuscrits de mathématiques de pointe pendant un certain temps. L'entonnoir est lié à une combinaison de facteurs : 1. L'impact augmente avec l'ambition, la taille du problème et l'horizon. Une question avec une réponse d'un paragraphe stresse à peine le système. Il faut un réservoir de problèmes grands et difficiles qui vous tiennent vraiment à cœur. Cet aspect pilote la dimension consommateur/professionnel de l'entonnoir. 2. Parfois, j'ai essayé de l'adoucir un peu, par exemple en demandant "80% du chemin vers l'ASD-STE100" car la spécification est assez stricte. Mais encore mieux : Diagrammes / images. Au lieu d'écrire, demandez à votre LLM de créer un diagramme. Ceux-ci peuvent être beaucoup plus faciles à traiter, à analyser et à comprendre. Mais encore mieux : Pages Web. Demandez une sortie "en HTML" pour obtenir une page web magnifique et interactive. Les LLM deviennent très bons en frontend et peuvent créer de belles expériences, des animations, etc. Mais encore mieux : Vidéos explicatives. Les règles concernant l'ampleur et la rapidité de croissance de ces entreprises sont en train d'être réécrites. Mais au début, la technologie est non prouvée, les ressources nécessaires sont énormes et la vision semble invraisemblable. actu.text_fr: Nous allons passer beaucoup plus de temps à essayer de comprendre les sorties des modèles de langage. Quelques réflexions, astuces et conseils : Écriture. Quelque chose qui m'a réussi : Demandez à votre LLM d'expliquer quelque chose en ASD-STE100, c'est une spécification de langage contrôlé développée à l'origine pour la documentation de maintenance aérospatiale. Les LLM sont bien versés dans ce langage et il impose de fortes contraintes sur un style d'écriture clair que je trouve souvent beaucoup plus lisible. Parfois, j'ai essayé de l'adoucir un peu, par exemple en demandant "80% du chemin vers l'ASD-STE100" car la spécification est assez stricte. Mais encore mieux : Diagrammes / images. Au lieu d'écrire, demandez à votre LLM de créer un diagramme. Ceux-ci peuvent être beaucoup plus faciles à traiter, à analyser et à comprendre. Mais encore mieux : Pages Web. Demandez une sortie "en HTML" pour obtenir une page web magnifique et interactive. Les LLM deviennent très bons en frontend et peuvent créer de belles expériences, des animations, etc. Mais encore mieux : Vidéos explicatives. Le format de sortie sur lequel je suis le plus optimiste est les vidéos explicatives entièrement personnalisées / sur mesure générées sur n'importe quel sujet arbitraire. Expérimentez avec des choses comme "Créez une vidéo explicative de style 3b1b sur X. Utilisez ma clé API ElevenLabs pour la narration audio". (vous auriez besoin d'une clé API pour cette dernière ou vous pouvez demander à votre LLM de vous trouver des alternatives gratuites décentes qui utilisent votre calcul local). Cela commence vraiment à fonctionner ! En résumé : - À mesure que les LLM s'amélioreront, ils feront de plus en plus de travail de manière autonome, et une grande partie de notre travail montera dans les abstractions, vers la supervision et la compréhension. - Heureusement, les LLM peuvent aussi aider ici car, à mesure que l'intelligence et le code sont de plus en plus abondants, vous pouvez demander de grands artefacts logiciels personnalisés et jetables (par exemple, des applications web, des vidéos explicatives) qu'il n'aurait jamais été logique de créer auparavant. Poussez les limites ici et vous serez surpris.
actu.text_original: We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks: Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better: Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better: Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better: Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work! In summary: - As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding. - Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

actu.text_fr: Je dépoussière ce tweet d'avril parce que ce fossé de compréhension des capacités des LLM *s'élargit*. Ce n'est plus "deux groupes de personnes qui parlent sans se comprendre" mais plutôt un entonnoir très étroit. - On estime à environ 6 milliards de personnes (environ 75% de la population) qui n'ont presque pas été en contact avec les LLM. - Environ 1 à 2 milliards (~20%) sont des utilisateurs occasionnels et peu fréquents de produits gratuits de type ChatGPT. Ce groupe voit des chatbots un peu maladroits et les traite comme une meilleure recherche Google, une aide à l'écriture, etc. Peut-être qu'un agent essaie de vous réserver un vol. J'ai des amis non-techniciens qui (raisonnablement, à mon avis) disent qu'ils n'y voient pas beaucoup d'utilité. Même de nombreux professionnels en dehors des mathématiques et du code sont à ce niveau. Par exemple, les dirigeants et de nombreuses autres fonctions passent beaucoup de leur temps à parler à d'autres personnes, donc même s'ils comprennent intellectuellement ce qui se passe, c'est de seconde main et un peu abstrait. - Nous arrivons maintenant à l'utilisation professionnelle des LLM de pointe dans les mathématiques et le code. Quelque part autour de 20 millions de personnes (0,2%) voient directement que de grands projets complexes qui leur prenaient des semaines/mois peuvent maintenant être réalisés par des agents avec une simple instruction (un "prompt"). Construire des applications, copier des applications, traduire des applications, décompiler des applications à partir de binaires... Tout cela s'est produit très rapidement et récemment – il y a moins d'un an, j'écrivais du code manuellement, tapant des commandes informatiques mémorisées dans un éditeur de code caractère par caractère, appuyant occasionnellement sur Tab pour compléter un petit morceau de code. - Et enfin, nous arrivons aux quelque 5 000 personnes (~0,00006%) ayant accès à des systèmes de pointe en interne. Le monde extérieur a vu l'aperçu. Cela ressemble à des essaims de milliers d'agents collaborant pendant des semaines sur des mégaprojets logiciels : création de failles "zero days", exécution de cyberattaques et de défenses à la vitesse de la machine, découverte de nouvelles sciences, avancement de la frontière des mathématiques. Des choses qui auraient pris des années de travail aux meilleurs professionnels de l'industrie. Pendant ce temps, l'examen et la compréhension humaine commencent à prendre du retard. Par exemple, les gens sont toujours impliqués dans "l'archéologie" de l'incident OpenAI-HF d'il y a plusieurs mois. Les mathématiciens pourraient se pencher sur les 722 manuscrits de mathématiques de pointe pendant un certain temps. L'entonnoir est lié à une combinaison de facteurs : 1. L'impact augmente avec l'ambition, la taille du problème et l'horizon. Une question avec une réponse d'un paragraphe stresse à peine le système. Il faut un réservoir de problèmes grands et difficiles qui vous tiennent vraiment à cœur. Cet aspect pilote la dimension consommateur/professionnel de l'entonnoir. 2. L'irrégularité du système (sur laquelle j'ai beaucoup écrit séparément). La capacité atteint des sommets dans les domaines qui sont numériques, vérifiables et économiquement précieux. C'est parce que la capacité des LLM émerge de l'apprentissage par renforcement sur des récompenses vérifiables dans un mélange d'environnements curatés et motivés par le potentiel de revenus. Cet aspect pilote principalement la dimension du domaine (par exemple, mathématiques et code) de l'entonnoir. 3. L'accès. Niveau gratuit, niveau payant, interne. C'est donc l'étrangeté du moment. Le grand public n'a pour la plupart pas interagi avec ces systèmes. Quand ils l'ont fait, cela ressemble à un chatbot maladroit. La majorité des professionnels ne voient encore qu'une amélioration modeste. Et une petite tranche de professionnels connaît le vertige de la courbe qui monte verticalement. Et il est tout cela se passe en même temps. Andrej Karpathy (@karpathy) À en juger par ma TL, il y a un fossé croissant dans la compréhension des capacités de l'IA. Le premier problème, je pense, est lié à la récence et au niveau d'utilisation. Je pense que beaucoup de gens ont essayé le niveau gratuit de ChatGPT l'année dernière et l'ont laissé informer un peu trop leurs opinions sur l'IA un peu trop. C'est un groupe de réactions qui se moquent de diverses bizarreries des modèles, des hallucinations, etc. Oui j'ai aussi vu les vidéos virales du mode vocal avancé d'OpenAI se trompant sur des requêtes simples comme "dois-je conduire ou marcher jusqu'au lave-auto". Le fait est que ces modèles gratuits et anciens/dépréciés ne reflètent pas la capacité des dernières générations de modèles agentiques de pointe de cette année, en particulier OpenAI Codex et Claude Code. Mais cela m'amène au deuxième problème. Même si les gens payaient 200$/mois pour utiliser les modèles de pointe, une grande partie des capacités sont relativement "pointues" dans des domaines très techniques. Les requêtes typiques concernant la recherche, l'écriture, les conseils, etc. ne sont *pas* le domaine qui a connu les progrès les plus notables et les plus spectaculaires en matière de capacités. En partie, cela est dû aux détails techniques de l'apprentissage par renforcement et à son utilisation de récompenses vérifiables. Mais en partie, c'est aussi parce que ces cas d'utilisation ne sont pas suffisamment prioritaires par les entreprises dans leur optimisation car ils ne génèrent pas autant de valeur en dollars. Les mines d'or sont ailleurs, et l'attention suit. Ce qui m'amène au deuxième groupe de personnes, qui *à la fois* 1) paient et utilisent les modèles agentiques de pointe (OpenAI Codex / Claude Code) et 2) le font professionnellement dans des domaines techniques comme la programmation, les mathématiques et la recherche. Ce groupe de personnes est soumis à la plus grande quantité de "psychose de l'IA" car les améliorations récentes dans ces domaines cette année ont été tout simplement stupéfiantes. Lorsque vous donnez un terminal informatique à l'un de ces modèles, vous pouvez maintenant les voir résoudre des problèmes de programmation qui vous prendraient normalement des jours/semaines de travail. C'est ce deuxième groupe de personnes qui accorde une bien plus grande gravité aux capacités, à leur pente et aux diverses répercussions cybernétiques. TLDR les gens de ces deux groupes parlent sans se comprendre. Il est vraiment simultanément vrai que le "mode vocal avancé" gratuit et, je pense, légèrement orphelin (?) d'OpenAI se trompera sur les questions les plus stupides de vos bobines Instagram et *en même temps*, le modèle Codex payant et de plus haut niveau d'OpenAI passera 1 heure à restructurer de manière cohérente une base de code entière, ou à trouver et exploiter des vulnérabilités dans des systèmes informatiques. Cette partie fonctionne vraiment et a fait des progrès spectaculaires grâce à 2 propriétés : 1) ces domaines offrent des fonctions de récompense explicites qui sont vérifiables, ce qui signifie qu'elles sont facilement adaptables à l'apprentissage par renforcement (par exemple, tests unitaires réussis oui ou non, en contraste avec l'écriture, qui est beaucoup plus difficile à juger explicitement), mais aussi 2) elles sont beaucoup plus précieuses dans des contextes B2B, ce qui signifie que la plus grande partie de l'équipe se concentre sur leur amélioration. Voilà où nous en sommes. — https://nitter.kareem.one/karpathy/status/2042334451611693415#m
actu.text_original: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while. The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal. So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time. Andrej Karpathy (@karpathy) Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability. The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. This is a group of reactions laughing at various quirks of the models, hallucinations, etc. Yes I also saw the viral videos of OpenAI's Advanced Voice mode fumbling simple queries like "should I drive or walk to the carwash". The thing is that these free and old/deprecated models don't reflect the capability in the latest round of state of the art agentic models of this year, especially OpenAI Codex and Claude Code. But that brings me to the second issue. Even if people paid $200/month to use the state of the art models, a lot of the capabilities are relatively "peaky" in highly technical areas. Typical queries around search, writing, advice, etc. are *not* the domain that has made the most noticeable and dramatic strides in capability. Partly, this is due to the technical details of reinforcement learning and its use of verifiable rewards. But partly, it's also because these use cases are not sufficiently prioritized by the companies in their hillclimbing because they don't lead to as much $$$ value. The goldmines are elsewhere, and the focus comes along. So that brings me to the second group of people, who *both* 1) pay for and use the state of the art frontier agentic models (OpenAI Codex / Claude Code) and 2) do so professionally in technical domains like programming, math and research. This group of people is subject to the highest amount of "AI Psychosis" because the recent improvements in these domains as of this year have been nothing short of staggering. When you hand a computer terminal to one of these models, you can now watch them melt programming problems that you'd normally expect to take days/weeks of work. It's this second group of people that assigns a much greater gravity to the capabilities, their slope, and various cyber-related repercussions. TLDR the people in these two groups are speaking past each other. It really is simultaneously the case that OpenAI's free and I think slightly orphaned (?) "Advanced Voice Mode" will fumble the dumbest questions in your Instagram's reels and *at the same time*, OpenAI's highest-tier and paid Codex model will go off for 1 hour to coherently restructure an entire code base, or find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. This part really works and has made dramatic strides because 2 properties: 1) these domains offer explicit reward functions that are verifiable meaning they are easily amenable to reinforcement learning training (e.g. unit tests passed yes or no, in contrast to writing, which is much harder to explicitly judge), but also 2) they are a lot more valuable in b2b settings, meaning that the biggest fraction of the team is focused on improving them. So here we are. — https://nitter.kareem.one/karpathy/status/2042334451611693415#m

idees.text_fr: Nous publions notre rapport d'intelligence sur les menaces le plus détaillé à ce jour. Il couvre la manière dont les gens ont tenté d'abuser de Claude—pour des cyberattaques, des opérations d'influence, de la surveillance, la biologie et la fabrication d'armes—et comment nous les avons trouvées et arrêtées. Nous avons interrompu toutes les opérations du rapport et utilisé les leçons tirées pour renforcer nos mesures de sécurité. Le cas échéant, nous avons également partagé nos découvertes avec les autorités et d'autres entreprises d'IA. Ces cas ne sont pas typiques : nous mettons en évidence certaines des utilisations abusives les plus sophistiquées que nous ayons vues. Mais il est particulièrement important d'en discuter, car ils nous montrent où se dirige l'utilisation abusive de l'IA, où nos mesures de sécurité fonctionnent et où elles doivent être améliorées. Nous publions ce rapport afin que d'autres puissent repérer la même activité sur leurs propres plateformes, et afin que nous puissions donner au public une vision plus claire de la manière dont les menaces émergentes se développent. idees.text_original: I’m starting a new early-stage AI fund, doing what I love: partnering with founders from company formation on bold bets, long before consensus. The fund’s LPs will include Sequoia, Jeff Dean, Sachin Katti, Philip Wong (my Stanford professor and Chief Scientist adviser to TSMC), and others whose work has shaped our industry and how I think about AI’s future. I’ll remain a partner at Sequoia and keep serving on my boards on Sequoia’s behalf. Sequoia has been my home for the past 11 years. I joined as the youngest investor the firm had ever hired. I grew up here. Through years of intense debate and shared work, I found lifelong mentors and friends who took me under their wing and taught me this craft. They taught me to aim high and take big swings. I’ll carry that into what I build: outsized ambition, relentless truth-seeking and curiosity, and a refusal to become complacent. Working alongside founders has made me want to build something of my own: a firm shaped from day one around the convictions I’ve developed over the past decade. Life has taught me not to take time for granted. This is how I want to spend mine. Why now We’re seeing a new way of building companies in today’s AI era. Research and products often advance together. A breakthrough can open a market or accelerate a business far faster than expected. Some companies require extraordinary capital and compute early on. Others reach meaningful scale with remarkably small teams. The rules for how big these businesses can get, and how fast, are being rewritten. But early on, the technology is unproven, the resources required enormous, and the vision seemingly implausible. This is what I love most: seeing the potential right from the beginning, and helping founders realize their full scale of ambition. More than ever, it starts with an extreme willingness to believe early, with bold, independent conviction in a founder’s technical insight before any product or market validation. Then, it means helping founders take the biggest swings, giving the rare, long-term patience to see those bets through uncertainty, ambiguity, and turbulence, and serving as a level head when the stakes are highest. I learned this kind of partnership at Sequoia. It’s the foundation of the firm I’m building. Believing before consensus My fascination with AI’s potential took root at Stanford in the early-to-mid 2010s, studying computer science and working in Andrew Ng’s lab. The friendships I formed connected me to a community whose people and ideas would help shape modern AI and build some of our generation’s defining companies. What stayed with me was the gap between what those people saw was possible and what the wider world could imagine. I’m drawn to founders pursuing ambitions that sound impossible today. I start with a simple question: “What if everything goes right?” Then we work backward together to make it happen. In 2023, Deepak and Abhinav set out to build a general-purpose robot brain at @SkildAI , before physical AI was a consensus bet. Their sim-to-real breakthroughs gave me conviction where earlier robotics approaches had fallen short. But the data flywheel required deployment at scale. We made commercialization as urgent as research and brought in strategic partners like NVIDIA and SoftBank to support the ambition. Three years in, Skild is advancing the frontier of physical AI with nine figures in annualized revenue. In 2024, Ioannis and Misha founded @reflection_ai with an insight into scaling reinforcement learning. As that grew into the ambition to build a Western frontier lab for open models, the hard question was how a startup competes with labs spending tens of billions. An introduction to NVIDIA and many compute calls and recruiting events later, the team has built Beam, now one of the leading US open models. In 2025, Anna et Azalia, the co-creators of AlphaChip, founded @RicursiveAI to design models and hardware together. From day one, we made early customers and ecosystem partners a priority. Today, they are showing order-of-magnitude improvements on real workloads, working with some of the industry’s most consequential players, and reaching a defining inflection point. The ambition keeps growing as these companies scale. @linear has always had a kind of magic to it. Now it’s the system a new generation of AI companies builds on, for teams and agents alike. @tavus saw early that we’d one day talk to AI the way we talk to each other. Today, it’s building the human computing interface for a world of AI colleagues. @Mach_Industries began as hydrogen experiments in an MIT dorm room. It has since become one of the most exciting next-generation defense companies. Making the ambition possible Being a first believer is only the beginning. Compute falls through. A deep-pocketed incumbent makes your mission its top priority. A breakthrough changes the opportunity and the capital required overnight. These are stomach-churning moments, and early belief carries a responsibility to help make the bet work. This is the partnership I love: turning the full ambition into concrete steps. Raising capital, securing compute and strategic partners, recruiting exceptional people, and winning the first customers together. Thinking several moves ahead while solving what’s in front of us. And as breakthroughs open new possibilities, helping founders dream even bigger. Thank you To the founders I’ve worked with: thank you for trusting me and Sequoia to be your first partner and first believer. It’s been the joy of a lifetime, and I can’t wait to keep building together. Thank you to Alfred and Pat for your leadership of Sequoia and your support of my next chapter. To Roelof, for bringing me into Sequoia and believing in me from the beginning. Alfred and Roelof, you have been mentors in investing and in life. So much of what I know, and the investor I’ve become, comes from your guidance and generosity over the years. To Bill, for the close partnership and wealth of knowledge, always wrapped in humility. To Shaun, for showing me how to think deeply and imaginatively. To Michael Moritz, for inspiring 22-year-old me to dream big. To Doug, for teaching me to keep things simple. To Bogie and Jess, for bringing joy to the everyday and perspective on what matters. And to all my Sequoia teammates, for the friendship, camaraderie, and lessons I’ll carry with me. To my family, especially my husband and my brother, who have each started companies of their own: thank you for giving me the courage to take this leap. Let’s get to work!

One in which getting the safety and security challenges of increasingly capable AI right has to become a central priority. So I’ll be returning to OpenAI, joining @merettm to help chart a path through these challenges. There’s much work to do, so let’s get going.
idees.decryptage: Aleksander Madry, expert en sécurité, annonce son retour chez OpenAI pour se concentrer sur les défis de sécurité et de fiabilité des IA de plus en plus puissantes.

outils.text_fr: Gemini #1 sur AAv5 ??? cela me donne envie d'ouvrir @antigravity pour la première fois depuis longtemps. Je suis en train de faire un examen anticipé, je vous ferai un rapport bientôt. si Google réussit cela, c'est officiellement la saison du retour en force avec Meta, Grok et maintenant GDM redevenant cool. @saranormous a parlé de neurodiversité des modèles l'année dernière. nous avons environ 2 fois plus de laboratoires de pointe que lors de sa dernière apparition sur la scène aie. un contre-exemple absolument bizarre à la leçon amère. Artificial Analysis (@ArtificialAnlys) Gemini 4 Carbon de Google est le nouveau numéro 1 sur l'Index d'Intelligence v5 d'Artificial Analysis, et deuxième seulement derrière Claude Opus 5.5 sur l'Index d'Agents de Codage d'Artificial Analysis. Gemini 4 Carbon obtient un score de 59 sur l'Intelligence Index v5, grâce à des performances de pointe en raisonnement complexe, en connaissance et en tâches scientifiques. Il réalise également d'importants gains en codage et en travail de connaissance, notamment par rapport aux autres modèles Gemini, mais il n'est pas leader dans tous ces domaines. Comme pour le lancement de Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 4 Carbon est en cours de déploiement auprès d'utilisateurs sélectionnés et n'est pas encore disponible publiquement. Google offre une réduction de lancement de 50%, sans date de fin confirmée. Tous nos graphiques et chiffres utilisent les prix standard pour Gemini 4 Carbon et Argon. Résultats clés pour Gemini 4 Carbon avec un raisonnement élevé : ➤ Gemini 4 Carbon est en tête de l'Intelligence Index v5, avec le score n°1 dans 4 des 9 évaluations de l'Index : HLE-Diamond, Terminal-Bench-Science, AA-Omniscience, AutomationBench-AA. Carbon réalise des gains substantiels ailleurs mais n'est pas leader en codage et en travail de connaissance ➤ Derrière seulement Claude Opus 5.5 sur les agents de codage : Avec Antigravity CLI, Gemini 4 Carbon (élevé) obtient un score de 59, à seulement 3 points derrière Claude Code avec Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 62) sur l'Index d'Agents de Codage d'Artificial Analysis. Carbon se classe deuxième sur Terminal-Bench 4.0 (64%) et FrontierCode v1.1 (51%), derrière Claude Opus 5.5 (max) à 56%. Google a historiquement sous-performé dans ce domaine, et cette amélioration se démarque ➤ Travail de connaissance agentique amélioré, mais pas encore leader : Sur AA-Briefcase, Gemini 4 Carbon (élevé) obtient 1609 Elo, une amélioration de 126 points par rapport à Gemini 4 Argon (élevé, 1483), mais reste derrière des modèles tels que Grok 4.7 (xhigh, 1638), Muse Wonder (max, 1659) et Kimi K3.1 Pro (1678). Le gain le plus important provient de la présentation, en hausse de 293 Elo à 1598, parallèlement à une amélioration de 120 points de la qualité analytique à 1671 ➤ Coût par tâche inférieur à Claude Opus 5.5 pour une intelligence globale comparable : Gemini 4 Carbon coûte 7,76 $ par tâche de l'Intelligence Index, ~23% de moins que Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 10,04 $) mais ~1,2 fois GPT-6 Astra (max, 6,25 $). Il utilise 123 000 jetons de sortie par tâche, 29% de moins que Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 173 000). Au même prix standard de 4 $/20 $, son coût par tâche est en ligne avec Gemini 4 Argon (7,68 $), tout en obtenant 9 points de plus sur l'Intelligence Index ➤ Score AA-Omniscience v1.1 de pointe, avec une faible hallucination : Gemini 4 Carbon obtient 54 sur notre AA-Omniscience v1.1 récemment mise à jour, 6 points devant Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 48) et 8 points devant Gemini 4 Argon (46). La précision (% correct) augmente de 10 points par rapport à Argon à 58%, tandis que son taux d'hallucination passe de 4% à 11%. C'est toujours le deuxième plus bas de tous les modèles, derrière seulement Argon, comparé à 50% pour Claude Opus 5.5 (max) et GPT-6 Astra (max) Détails clés du modèle : ➤ Fenêtre contextuelle : 1 million de jetons ➤ Multimodalité : Entrée texte, image, vidéo et parole, avec sortie texte ➤ Prix : 4 $/20 $ par million de jetons d'entrée/sortie, le même que le prix standard de Gemini 4 Argon, avec une réduction de 50%. Les jetons d'entrée mis en cache bénéficient d'une réduction de 95% (0,20 $ par million) Félicitations à l'équipe @GoogleDeepMind ! — http://nitter.jaydenha.uk/ArtificialAnlys/status/2115494553780367384#m

Artificial Analysis (@ArtificialAnlys) Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, and second only to Claude Opus 5.5 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index Gemini 4 Carbon scores 59 on Intelligence Index v5, driven by leading performance in complex reasoning, knowledge, and scientific tasks. It also has large gains in coding and knowledge work, particularly when compared to other Gemini models, but it is not leading in all these areas. As with launch of Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 4 Carbon is being rolled out to selected users and is not yet publicly available. Google is offering a 50% launch discount, with no confirmed end date. All our charts and figures use standard pricing for both Gemini 4 Carbon and Argon. Key results for Gemini 4 Carbon with high reasoning: ➤ Gemini 4 Carbon leads the Intelligence Index v5, with the #1 score in 4 of the 9 Index evaluations: HLE-Diamond, Terminal-Bench-Science, AA-Omniscience, AutomationBench-AA. Carbon makes substantial gains elsewhere but is not leading in coding and knowledge work ➤ Behind only Claude Opus 5.5 on coding agents: With Antigravity CLI, Gemini 4 Carbon (high) scores 59 only 3 points behind Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 62) on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index. Carbon ranks second on both Terminal-Bench 4.0 (64%) and FrontierCode v1.1 (51%), behind Claude Opus 5.5 (max) at 56%. Google has historically underperformed in this area and so this improvement stands out ➤ Improved agentic knowledge work, but not yet leading: On AA-Briefcase, Gemini 4 Carbon (high) scores 1609 Elo, a 126-point improvement over Gemini 4 Argon (high, 1483), but still behind models including Grok 4.7 (xhigh, 1638), Muse Wonder (max, 1659) and Kimi K3.1 Pro (1678). The largest gain comes from Presentation, up 293 Elo to 1598, alongside a 120-point improvement in Analytical Quality to 1671 ➤ Lower Cost per Task than Claude Opus 5.5 for comparable overall intelligence: Gemini 4 Carbon costs $7.76 per Intelligence Index task, ~23% less than Claude Opus 5.5 (max, $10.04) but ~1.2x GPT-6 Astra (max, $6.25). It uses 123k output tokens per task, 29% fewer than Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 173k). At the same $4/$20 standard pricing, its Cost per Task is in line with Gemini 4 Argon ($7.68), while scoring 9 points higher on the Intelligence Index ➤ Leading AA-Omniscience v1.1 score, with low hallucination: Gemini 4 Carbon scores 54 on our recently updated AA-Omniscience v1.1, 6 points ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 48) and 8 points ahead of Gemini 4 Argon (46). Accuracy (% correct) rises 10 points over Argon to 58%, while its hallucination rate rises from 4% to 11%. This is still the second lowest of any model, behind only Argon, compared with 50% for both Claude Opus 5.5 (max) and GPT-6 Astra (max) Key model details: ➤ Context Window: 1M tokens ➤ Multimodality: Text, image, video, and speech input, with text output ➤ Pricing: $4/$20 per 1M input/output tokens, the same as Gemini 4 Argon’s standard pricing, with a 50% discount. Cached input tokens receive a 95% discount ($0.20 per 1M) Congratulations to the @GoogleDeepMind team! — http://nitter.jaydenha.uk/ArtificialAnlys/status/2115494553780367384#m
